deep.reconstruction:
The page has no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is the first page of a section headed 'Allgemein Mathematisch-Philosophische Bemerkungen' (general mathematical-philosophical remarks), continuing the loose aphoristic notes of the previous page (on the general and his marksmanship, the Gartenfrau and geometric intuition, word versus thought as 'the invariant').

Content, paraphrased:
(1) To separate 'geometers' and 'analysts' as purely externally as Klein does is like a Privy Councillor of the Ministry of Culture sorting people by 'directions'. The phrase rendered 'wie Klein einsieht' is uncertain; it is probably 'wie Klein es thut'.
(2) Counterexample from the calculus of variations, in Hilbert's ordering:
- Jacobi, 'the geometer', created the theory of shortest lines. Mathematically this means geodesics, conjugate points and the Jacobi condition from the transformation of the second variation (1836/37).
- Weierstrass, 'the geometer', has a calculus of variations that is 'truly geometric'. This means his field-of-extremals, E-function and sufficiency theory, presented in Berlin lectures from 1879 on.
- Between them stand the 'analysts' Clebsch and (an interlinear addition) Hesse. For them only formally elegant formulas and computations matter. The words 'und der Analytiker Hesse' were added and 'Geometer' was struck out, so the relative pronoun became plural ('denen').
(3) Restated sharply: Jacobi before and Weierstrass after proved themselves true geometers with 'mighty, pioneering achievements of genuinely geometric nature'. Clebsch is the 'one-sidedly formalistic analyst' with his 'monstrous transformations of the second variation'. This refers to Clebsch's 1858 Crelle papers reducing the second variation for general (multi-function, constrained) problems.
(4) Aphorisms on general ideas versus detail: 'The strongest genius can perish in the struggle with particulars and trivia; the general idea is the sceptre of kings. If we throw the builder of the Kaiser Wilhelm into the middle of the ocean, he will drown.' The ship is very probably the liner Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse (1897), which suggests a dating of about 1897 or later.
(5) 'Should Moltke take part in the shooting drills? Many a ...' This continues onto the next sheet and echoes the previous page's remark about the general who shoots badly.

No mathematical steps exist to reconstruct. The implicit mathematical referents (Jacobi's accessory equation and conjugate-point condition, Weierstrass's field theory, Clebsch's reduction of the second variation) are supplied by me as context only.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible: the page contains no derivations.

Historiographically, Hilbert's portrait of Clebsch as a pure formalist is polemical. Clebsch's 1858 work was a serious general treatment of the second variation for problems with several functions and side conditions; it was later simplified (e.g. by A. Mayer). Calling Jacobi's 1837 result 'the theory of shortest lines' is loose shorthand for his geodesic and conjugate-point work.

deep.surprise_reason: A private, aphoristic opinion page with no mathematics. Hilbert's preference for Weierstrass's geometric field theory is consistent with his own later invariant-integral work (1900). The sharp private judgment against Clebsch and Hesse, and the jab at Klein's classification, are mildly interesting biographical colour but not surprising.

checkable.asserts: Context only, not on the page: the Jacobi accessory equation for geodesics on the unit sphere along a great circle is u''+u=0. Its solution vanishing at 0 is sin(x), whose next zero (the first conjugate point) is at pi.
Context only: the zeros of sin are 0 and pi, i.e. the conjugate point of a great-circle arc lies at the antipode.
